textRun.content: 001 · How memory works — MEMORY-A2
Content: Revised draft · Approval: Guy’s opening edits accepted; revised remainder pending review · Built version: — · Verified version: — · Revision: 2 (30 October 2026)
OUTCOME: Experience how a familiar meaning can make new information easier to remember, then apply the same idea to learning Hebrew.
CONNECT TO: Familiar dates and events provide meaning for a number that initially looks random.
PREREQUISITES:
None.
PLAN:
https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1jlSH8qDBt3nwv90J_2IKkL-pzbRx3USW522KqtXR0Nc/edit#gid=102626001&range=A4:M4

SOURCES / ADAPTATION: Guy’s original presentation, slides 7–9 (0704177609112001, ten seconds, familiar dates and associative memory), with the letter connection on slide 10. Source: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ImMGqVDWT8BMN63xay1-DT7ug3Z1W9mr/view. Guy’s opening and Adam text were accepted verbatim on 30 October 2026. New transitions, exercise wording and interaction specifications below adapt his demonstration.

DESIGN DECISIONS: Guy’s 30 October correction supersedes the picture exercise in the earlier A2 draft. Preserve his established number-and-dates demonstration and personal teaching voice. Explain the experience before naming the principle, then connect it to Hebrew and everyday learning. This introductory demonstration does not change the deferred Hebrew numbers sequence.
Learn — exact text and embedded interactions
Screen 1: Welcome to Hebleo · MEMORY-A2.learn.try-first
LEARNER TEXT:
Welcome to Hebleo, the smart way to learn Hebrew. This course is the result of a 10+ year long journey, combining many years of experience in:
Learning languages independently on a self-paced basis and seeing what works and what doesn’t first-hand,
Teaching Hebrew as a tutor and developing materials along the way, optimizing them with each new student with different approaches, and seeing what works well long-term
Getting an
M.Sc
. in Cognitive Science. It has helped me understand how to optimize learning in general and language learning in particular.
[NEXT PAGE — learner selects Continue]
Screen 2: Adam · MEMORY-A2.learn.adam-study

This led to a case study I did with a student named Adam. He came to me with Zero Hebrew knowledge, but similar scientific background. After I explained the method to him, he became intrigued and we decided to test how long it would take him to get to a level where we would be able to generally hold Hebrew conversations together. For an English speaker learning Hebrew, this usually takes around 500 hours. For Adam, using the methodology that is at the core of Hebleo, it took around
70 hours
. This means that his pace was over 7x higher than the norm.
Let’s briefly demonstrate some of the underlying concepts used in the course that improve your learning and memory. Understanding them can help you use them in your personal life as well!
[NEXT PAGE — learner selects Continue]
Screen 3: A quick memory experiment · MEMORY-A2.learn.number-round
LEARNER TEXT:
Let’s try a quick experiment. I’m going to show you a number for ten seconds. Try to remember as much of it as you can without writing it down. When it disappears, type what you remember.
Ready? Press Play to begin.

[PLACEHOLDER / AUTHOR INSTRUCTION] TIMED DISPLAY MEMORY-NUMBER: show the exact string 0704177609112001 for 10,000 ms after Play, then hide it before enabling recall. Display digits left to right; do not show dates, event labels, grouping or the answer before the first attempt. Never autoplay.

[PLACEHOLDER / AUTHOR INSTRUCTION] CONTROL: Play → ten-second display → hidden-number recall → submit attempt or “I can’t remember yet” → Continue to the explanation. Replay starts a fresh attempt. An untimed study option is available. For nonvisual access, provide an on-demand spoken digit sequence and hide the accessible number before recall; this is an alternative experience, not a comparable timed score. Leaving the page cancels the timer. No pass threshold or speed comparison.
MEMORY-A2.embedded.number-first — typed recall
LEARNER PROMPT: What was the number? Type as much as you remember, then continue.

ANSWER / ACCEPTED MODEL: 0704177609112001. Store and compare as a string, never as a numeric value; leading zeroes matter. Ignore spaces between digit groups. This first attempt is ungraded; reveal the number only on the next screen.
FEEDBACK: Keep your attempt for comparison. In a moment, I’ll show you a different way to think about the same number.
[NEXT PAGE — learner selects Continue]
Screen 4: Give the number meaning · MEMORY-A2.learn.connection
LEARNER TEXT:
That was quite a lot of digits to remember! Now let’s look at the same number in a different way:
These dates use American month–day–year order: July 4, 1776, and September 11, 2001.
The first is the date of the American Declaration of Independence; the second is the date of the September 11 attacks. If you already know those events, the digits now connect to something familiar.

We haven’t changed the number. We’ve changed what it means to you: instead of sixteen unrelated digits, you can think of two dates you already know. If those dates are unfamiliar, the connection will be less helpful. The useful starting point is something you already know.
[NEXT PAGE — learner selects Continue]
Screen 5: What made the difference? · MEMORY-A2.learn.meaning
LEARNER TEXT:
While we’ll use all 3 principles to enhance our learning, right now I want to focus on the third one:

: connect new information to established old information. You already have a great deal of knowledge to build on from your life experience. A useful connection gives the new information a place in that knowledge. At first we’ll connect brand new Hebrew concepts to things you’re already familiar with from English, and as we move forward we’ll connect new Hebrew concepts to older Hebrew concepts you’re already comfortable with.
Let’s check what changed in our experiment before you try the number again.

[PLACEHOLDER / AUTHOR INSTRUCTION] PAGE BREAK: keep the number, dates and first attempt on earlier screens. This screen asks about the method without displaying the recall answer. No new image asset is required. If they answer in reverse order, have a message prepared for it. If they answer without zeros or otherwise right numbers but wrong format (including wrong order) - have messages pointing out specifically what they got wrong.
MEMORY-A2.embedded.what-changed — multiple choice
LEARNER PROMPT: What changed when we recognised the two dates?
OPTIONS / TOKEN POOL:
A. Some of the digits were removed.
B. The same digits connected to familiar events.
C. The digits were rearranged into a different number.
ANSWER / ACCEPTED MODEL: The same digits connected to familiar events.
FEEDBACK after “Some of the digits were removed.”: All sixteen digits are still there. The dates give us a meaningful way to organise them.
FEEDBACK after “The same digits connected to familiar events.”: Exactly. We kept the information and connected it to something already familiar.
FEEDBACK after “The digits were rearranged into a different number.”: The order stayed the same. We recognised a meaning within it.
[NEXT PAGE — learner selects Continue]
Screen 6: Try the connection for yourself · MEMORY-A2.learn.return
LEARNER TEXT:

Let’s try again. Press Play to see the same number for ten seconds, this time with the two dates in mind. When it disappears, type what you remember. Think back to the events and see whether they help you recover the digits.

After checking your attempt, notice what helped you. Did you recall the dates, picture the events, or find a different connection? We’ll take this idea into the next lesson, where familiar images will help us connect Hebrew letter shapes to their sounds.
MEMORY-A2.embedded.number-return — typed recall
LEARNER PROMPT: After the number disappears, type it again using the connection you have just made.

[PLACEHOLDER / AUTHOR INSTRUCTION] REUSE MEMORY-NUMBER: the same ungrouped string, ten-second Play/Replay behavior, untimed and nonvisual alternatives. Earlier dates and answers stay hidden during recall. After submission or “I can’t remember yet”, Check reveals the exact number, the two date groups and the learner’s two attempts. Recall remains ungraded.
ANSWER / ACCEPTED MODEL: 0704177609112001. Accept spacing between digit groups; retain every digit in the original order, including the first zero.

FEEDBACK: Compare your attempt with 0704177609112001, or 07041776 · 09112001. If the dates helped, notice how the familiar events brought the digits back. If they didn’t, ask whether those events were already familiar enough to help you. You can replay or continue after comparing.
[NEXT PAGE — learner selects Continue]
Check — understanding
MEMORY-A2.check.useful-anchor — multiple choice
LEARNER PROMPT: When you use this idea to learn something new, what should you look for?
OPTIONS / TOKEN POOL:
A. A connection to something you already know.
B. The most complicated story you can invent.
C. A way to avoid ever practising it again.
ANSWER / ACCEPTED MODEL: A connection to something you already know.
FEEDBACK after “A connection to something you already know.”: Yes. Start with what’s familiar and use it to make sense of the new information.
FEEDBACK after “The most complicated story you can invent.”: Your connection can be simple. What matters is whether it helps you bring the new information back to mind.
FEEDBACK after “A way to avoid ever practising it again.”: A connection gives you a useful starting point. We’ll also practise retrieving what you learn and return to it later in the course.
Vocabulary — current learner display and author reference
No new vocabulary entries in this lesson. Letter shapes, sounds or memory materials are taught in Learn and practised in the exercises; do not add a lexical quota.
Apply — complete exercise set
MEMORY-A2.apply.personal-connection — self-check
LEARNER PROMPT: Think of a date you already know. How would knowing its meaning help you remember the digits? You can keep your example private and explain it to yourself.

ANSWER / ACCEPTED MODEL: Any familiar date with an explanation linking its meaning to its digits. Example: “New Year’s Day is January 1, so I can recover 01/01 by thinking of the start of the year.” This is a self-check with no single required date or wording.
FEEDBACK: Ask yourself: did I already know the event, and can thinking of it bring the date back to mind? The same idea can help with a new word, a name or something else you want to learn.
Continue — learner text

You’ve now tried one of the ideas behind Hebleo for yourself: connecting new information to something you already know. Next, we’ll use familiar images to help you learn your first four Hebrew letters. Let’s begin!
Author review and implementation record

AUTHOR REVIEW: Guy’s accepted opening and Adam account remain verbatim. The original presentation’s slide 4 names B1, while his new text says B2; this discrepancy is flagged in chat for his decision. The 500/70-hour comparison is Guy’s supplied account, not independently verified evidence or a promised learner outcome. Review the newly adapted transitions and exercises; verify the ten-second display, leading zero, hidden answers, replay, nonvisual/untimed alternatives and all choice feedback during implementation.
